utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber is now in session. Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-94-1-A-R77, the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic in a matter concerning allegations of contempt against prior counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I take it that the appearances are as before? Are there any changes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet is not here today but, Mr. Vujin, you are. Mr. Tadic, you can hear me? THE APPELLANT: [Nods]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber of this International Tribunal is now sitting to deliver its Judgement in an ancillary matter in this case involving allegations of contempt against a prior counsel of Dusko Tadic, namely, Mr. Milan Vujin of Belgrade, both of whom are in the Chamber today. The Judgement is unanimous. Before giving my comments concerning the case, it is necessary, however, to note for the record that the Appeals Chamber is sitting today with only four of its members, Judge Cassese being unavoidably absent. The Vice-President of the International Tribunal, Judge Mumba, acting in the absence of the President, has authorised the Chamber to deliver this Judgement in the absence of one of its members, pursuant to Rule 15 bis (D) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and an Order to that effect has been filed today. I note that Judge Cassese has heard all of the evidence in this matter and has participated fully in the deliberation and determination of the allegations, including the settlement of the Judgement. Copies of the Judgement, which is in writing, will be made available by the Registrar to the parties, including the interested parties, towards the end of this sitting. Following the practice of the Tribunal, I shall limit myself to introductory matters and shall not read out the text of the Judgement, save for the operative paragraph. I make it clear that the Judgement is set out in the text to be distributed. This statement is not the Judgement of the Appeals Chamber, except for the reading of the disposition of the Judgement. The allegations arise out of the alleged conduct of Mr. Vujin while he was assigned counsel, that is, paid for by the International Tribunal, in the early parts of the appeal in the case; that is to say, from mid 1997 until the assignment was terminated at the request of Mr. Dusko Tadic in November 1998. The allegations were first brought to the attention of the Appeals Chamber in late 1998. On 10 February 1999, the Appeals Chamber issued a Scheduling Order calling upon Mr. Vujin to answer allegations that he knowingly and wilfully intended to interfere with the administration of justice in this case. Attached to that Order were copies of statements on which the allegations were based. Dusko Tadic and the Office of the Prosecutor were both granted leave to appear as interested parties in these proceedings. The Appeals Chamber has heard much oral evidence in this case. Due to circumstances largely beyond its control, the hearings were spread over a period from March to November of last year. A total of 12 witnesses were summoned by the Appeals Chamber itself to testify as to the various events alleged in the statements, including Dusko Tadic and his assigned counsel during the trial, Mr. Wladimiroff. Mr. Vujin called a total of eight witnesses in his defence and also gave evidence himself at the close of his case. Pursuant to Rule 79 of the Rules, much of the evidence was heard in closed session for the protection of certain witnesses who were concerned as to possible retaliation against them and their families. The Orders granting those protective measures provided that the transcripts of the closed session testimony could be released after suitable redaction to protect the identity of those concerned. The Judgement includes Orders that such testimony and the related documentary evidence may be referred to publicly to the extent necessary to enable the Judgement to be comprehensible as a public document. During the hearings, evidence was heard that did not relate directly to the allegations of contempt as set out in the Scheduling Order but which reflected in various ways the events set out in the statements. This was done for the purpose of demonstrating a particular course of conduct or to explain the events that took place within the specified period. Mr. Vujin was at all times made aware of the case he had to meet. The evidence admitted by the Appeals Chamber relates to alleged conduct of Mr. Vujin which may be grouped as follows: (1) putting forward to the Appeals Chamber in support of an application for the admission of additional evidence on appeal ("the Rule 115 application"), a case which Mr. Vujin knew to be false; (i) in relation to the weight to be given to statements made by one Mlado Radic, a person indicted by the Tribunal; and (ii) in relation to the responsibility of another indicted person, Goran Borovnica, for the killing of two policemen of which Dusko Tadic was convicted; (2) manipulating proposed witnesses: (i) by seeking to avoid any identification by them of persons who may have been responsible for the crimes for which Dusko Tadic was convicted; and (ii) by persuading them to lie or withhold the truth when making statements in this connection; and (iii) bribing a witness to lie or withhold the truth. The first allegation arose out of materials submitted in support of the Rule 115 application. Among those materials were two statements from Mlado Radic, who was charged before the International Tribunal on a different indictment. The first of these asserted that it had been made shortly before Mlado Radic was arrested and that it had been made directly to Mr. Vujin in person; the second statement confirmed the first. It was established to the satisfaction of the Appeals Chamber that the first statement was made by Mlado Radic after his arrest, that it was made in the United Nations Detention Centre in The Hague, and that Mr. Vujin was not present at the time. The Appeals Chamber was also satisfied that Mr. Vujin knew the true circumstances surrounding the taking of the statement and that he submitted it intending it to be interpreted as it purported to be. The Appeals Chamber finds that Mr. Vujin did put forward a case in relation to that statement that he knew to be false in material respects. Also in the submission put forward in support of the Rule 115 application, Mr. Vujin emphasised the importance of the fact that one of the Defence witnesses at trial had testified that he had witnessed the killing of the two policemen and that they had been killed, not by Dusko Tadic, but by another accused, Goran Borovnica, who is thought to have since died. Evidence was led that demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Appeals Chamber that Mr. Vujin was aware that the trial witness had repudiated his story as to the person responsible for these killings and that, in connection with the appeal proceedings, that witness now asserted that the killer was a different person. The Appeals Chamber finds that Mr. Vujin did put forward a case in relation to the statement of that witness that he knew to be false in material respects. The second allegation, concerning manipulation of proposed witnesses, is based on claims that certain witnesses were instructed by Mr. Vujin not to name other persons who may have been implicated in the events in which Dusko Tadic was convicted and that certain witnesses were instructed to answer questions when being interviewed by other counsel as indicated by head signals given by Mr. Vujin, who was present when most of the statements were taken. The detailed evidence relating to these matters is described in the Judgement and I will not repeat it here. For the reasons set out in the Judgement, the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that the allegations as to manipulation of witnesses by seeking to prevent names from being named have been made out. The Appeals Chamber finds that the allegations as to the instruction to witnesses to answer questions according to head signals given by Mr. Vujin has not been made out. The third allegation is that of bribing a witness to lie or to withhold information. This allegation is based on the statement of Witness B that he had been paid 100 Deutschemarks, the equivalent of one month's wages, by Mr. Vujin after he gave a statement which did not identify other possible perpetrators of the crimes of which Dusko Tadic was convicted, but that he was not paid any money after a subsequent interview, made in the presence of co-counsel, in which he named one of the other possible perpetrators. Mr. Vujin did not deny giving Witness B money but asserted that the money had been given to help the witness because of the difficult financial and emotional circumstances in which the witness found himself at the time. A professional colleague of Mr. Vujin also testified that a second payment had been made to Witness B at a later time in circumstances unconnected with any interview. The Appeals Chamber does not make any finding of contempt in relation to this allegation. Certain of the allegations of contempt having been thus proved, it is necessary to consider punishment. The Appeals Chamber regards the contempt as serious. Courts and tribunals must rely upon the honesty of counsel in the conduct of cases before them. Counsel are granted various privileges by the law which are justified only if they can be trusted not to abuse them. The conduct of Mr. Vujin in this case strikes at the very heart of the criminal justice system. The maximum penalty prescribed by Rule 77 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence at the time of the contempt was a term of imprisonment not exceeding six months, or a fine of 20,000 guilders, or both. The Appeals Chamber has considered whether a term of imprisonment should be imposed but has decided that it would not be appropriate in this case. Nevertheless, a substantial fine is necessary to achieve the purposes for which punishment is imposed. There are also additional consequences which may flow from the finding of contempt and which the Appeals Chamber must take into consideration. Under the law of the Tribunal, the Registrar of the Tribunal maintains a list of counsel willing to be assigned to indigent suspects and accused. Mr. Vujin is on that list. In the opinion of the Appeals Chamber, the Registrar has a general power to strike the name of counsel from the list for serious professional misconduct and to report such conduct to the relevant professional body. A direction will therefore be given to the Registrar to consider striking the name of Mr. Vujin from the list and reporting his conduct to the appropriate professional body. The Appeals Chamber has determined the punishment to be imposed on the basis that the Registrar will so act and takes this into account. I shall now read the disposition of the Judgement of the Appeals Chamber. This is as follows: For the foregoing reasons, the Appeals Chamber unanimously: (1) finds the Respondent, Milan Vujin, in contempt of the Tribunal; (2) orders him to pay a fine of Dfl 15,000 to the Registrar of the Tribunal within 21 days, or within such further time as may be allowed upon application by the Respondent to the Appeals Chamber; (3) directs the Registrar of the Tribunal to consider striking the Respondent off the list of assigned counsel kept by her pursuant to Rule 45 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence and reporting his conduct as found by the Appeals Chamber to the professional body to which he belongs; (4) orders that copies of the following documents (redacted to comply with the relevant witness protection orders) be made public: (i) the Decision on Prosecution Request for Orders Regarding Defence Harassment and Intimidation of Witnesses of Potential Witnesses, 4 November 1998, together with the respective pleadings of the parties; and (ii) the Scheduling Order concerning allegations against prior counsel, 10 February 1999, but not the statements attached to it; and (5) orders that the material from the evidence given and in the documents tendered during any closed session of the hearing which has been referred to in the Judgement be made public so far as it has been so referred to. Done in both English and French, the English text being authoritative. I will ask the Registrar now to deliver copies of the Judgement to Mr. Vujin and to the interested parties. That concludes this sitting of the Appeals Chamber. The court stands adjourned.
